lesson:
# Pattern matching for DFM

Pattern matching scans a layout for every occurrence of a known problematic pattern. Patterns come from foundry libraries, from earlier hotspots, or from failure analysis. On a rasterized clip, matching is a sliding-window comparison; production engines hash windows and use topological signatures so that a full chip is searched in one pass. Rotations, mirrors and don't-care regions make one pattern cover a family of layouts.

## Exact matching of a raster pattern

Rasterize the layer into pixels (1 for metal) and slide a $p \times q$ pattern over every position of an $R \times C$ grid: there are $(R - p + 1)(C - q + 1)$ positions, and a match requires every pixel to agree. A $2 \times 2$ pattern over a $5 \times 5$ grid has 16 positions. Production matchers avoid pixel-by-pixel comparison by hashing each window (rolling hashes update in constant time as the window slides), or by encoding a clip's edge topology and dimensions so that matches survive small shifts.

## Orientation-invariant matching

Lithography treats a pattern and its rotations alike (for symmetric illumination), so a library entry should match in all orientations. The matcher generates the rotated versions (90, 180, 270 degrees; mirrors add four more) and counts positions where at least one matches. A position is counted once even if several orientations match it. A $2 \times 2$ pattern 10, 10 matches twice unrotated in a grid but eight times with rotations. Hash-based matchers store the canonical form of each pattern, the smallest hash over its orientations, so one lookup covers all of them.

## Don't-care pixels

Fuzzy patterns mark some pixels as don't-care, matching either value, so one entry covers every layout that agrees on the constrained pixels. A $3 \times 3$ pattern with three don't-cares compares six pixels per position. More don't-cares mean more matches, both real hotspots and false alarms. Library designers trade coverage against precision; learned detectors can be seen as a soft version of the same idea, where the model decides which pixels matter.

## Going deeper

The ICCAD 2012 CAD contest on fuzzy pattern matching for physical verification.

label: Double-patterning coloring conflicts
lesson:
# Double-patterning coloring conflicts

When features are packed tighter than one exposure can print, double patterning splits a layer onto two masks. Two features closer than the same-mask spacing must go on different masks, which makes mask assignment a graph 2-coloring problem. A layout is decomposable exactly when its conflict graph is bipartite, so double-patterning checks reduce to finding odd cycles.

## Building the conflict graph

Each feature is a vertex, and an edge joins two features closer than the same-mask spacing $S$, measured as Euclidean distance. With $S = 27$ nm, five features may produce two edges. Building the graph is a spacing check with a larger distance: candidate pairs from a sweep, then exact distances. Edges mean must-differ constraints. Features farther than $S$ from everything form isolated vertices, free to go on either mask, which the decomposer uses to balance density between the masks.

## Odd cycles

A graph is 2-colourable if and only if it has no odd cycle. A breadth-first search that alternates colours finds a same-colour edge exactly in a component that contains an odd cycle. Three features each closer than $S$ to the other two form a triangle, which no assignment can satisfy. Each component is checked separately, and each non-bipartite component is a double-patterning violation. Fixes are a layout change that removes an edge, or a stitch that splits one feature into two overlapping parts on different masks, where the process allows stitches.

## Counting mask assignments

A connected bipartite component has exactly two colourings: fix one vertex's mask and every other vertex is forced. Components are independent, so a graph with $c$ components, all bipartite, has $2^c$ assignments, counting isolated features as components; one odd component makes the count zero. Seven features in two components give 4 assignments. Decomposers use this freedom to balance pattern density between masks and to avoid stitches. Triple patterning raises the problem to 3-coloring, which is NP-complete in general, and changes the algorithms used.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Park, Xu and Yao, "Layout decomposition for double patterning lithography" (ICCAD, 2008).

label: Critical area of a layout
lesson:
# Critical area of a layout

Random particle defects cause shorts and opens. Whether a defect of a given size kills the chip depends on where it lands: the critical area is the area of positions where its centre causes a failure. Averaged over the defect size distribution and multiplied by defect density, it predicts yield. Critical-area analysis turns layout geometry into a yield number and drives DFM fixes such as wire spreading.

## Critical area at one defect size

For two long parallel wires with gap $s$ and run length $L$, a circular conducting defect of diameter $x$ shorts them when it touches both. For $x \le s$ that is impossible; for $x > s$ its centre must fall in a band of width $x - s$ between the wires, so $A_c(x) = L (x - s)$, ignoring end effects. With $L = 150$ um, $s = 135$ nm and $x = 220$ nm, the band is 85 nm wide and $A_c = 12.75$ square um. Opens are the dual: a missing-material defect of diameter $x$ cuts a wire of width $w$ when $x > w$, with $A_c = L(x - w)$.

## Averaging over defect sizes

Defect sizes follow a distribution, commonly $f(x) = 2 x_0^2 / x^3$ for $x \ge x_0$. The average short critical area of one gap is $\int_s^\infty L (x - s) f(x)\, dx = L x_0^2 / s$ for $s \ge x_0$. A bus of 4 wires has 3 gaps; with $L = 470$ um, $x_0 = 25$ nm and $s = 75$ nm the average is $3 \cdot 470 \cdot 625 / 75 / 1000 = 11.75$ square um, counting each gap separately. The $1 / s$ dependence explains why widening gaps pays off most where they are smallest.

## From critical area to yield

With defect density $D$ for a mechanism and average critical area $A_c$, the Poisson model gives yield $Y = e^{-D A_c}$. Units must agree: 13.3 square mm is 0.133 square cm, so with $D = 0.39$ defects per square cm, $D A_c = 0.05187$ and $Y = 94.95$ percent. Yields of independent mechanisms and layers multiply, so a chip's random-defect yield is the product over layers of shorts and opens. Clustered defects are modelled with negative binomial yield instead. Critical area is computed by Boolean and sizing operations, so it runs in the same engines as DRC.

## Going deeper

Stapper, "Modeling of integrated circuit defect sensitivities" (IBM Journal of Research and Development, 1983).

label: Recommended rules and DFM scoring
lesson:
# Recommended rules and DFM scoring

Beyond mandatory rules, foundries publish recommended rules: larger spacings, longer extensions, redundant vias. A layout that ignores them is legal but yields worse. DFM tools score how well a layout follows them and apply them where space allows. The engineering problem is choosing where the yield benefit justifies the area or routing cost.

## Scoring recommended rules

Recommended rules are scored, not passed or failed. A redundant-via score is the fraction of via locations with two or more cuts: 1534 of 2284 locations gives 67.2 percent. A spacing score is the fraction of neighbouring-wire gaps at or above the recommended value. Better scores weight each location by its yield impact, for example its critical area, so a long tightly spaced bus counts more than a short stub. The score is a metric to optimize, which makes it a natural objective for automated DFM passes and for agents.

## Wire spreading and critical area

Under the model where a gap's average short critical area is $L x_0^2 / s$, spreading two wires from 80 to 90 nm reduces it to $80 / 90$ of its value, an 11.1 percent reduction. The gain per nanometre is largest for the tightest gaps, so spreading targets minimum-spaced long runs where free tracks exist. Spreading can create new problems: it moves wires toward other neighbours, changes coupling, and may conflict with double-patterning colours. A DFM pass therefore re-runs DRC and extraction on what it changes.

## How tools use recommended rules

Routers apply recommended spacings and extensions opportunistically, where tracks are free, and fall back to minimum rules where routing is tight. Redundant-via insertion runs after routing, using leftover space. Recommended rules guard against specific failures: a longer metal extension past a via protects the enclosure from line-end shortening. Applying everything everywhere would cost area; the right policy applies rules where they buy the most yield, which is a cost-benefit decision the engine exposes as parameters.

label: Tape-out
lesson:
# Tape-out

Tape-out is the handoff of the final layout to the foundry for mask making. Everything physical verification does converges here: the signed-off stream, the agreed layer map, documented waivers, and proof that nothing changed after signoff. Mistakes found after tape-out cost masks and months, so the handoff is a checklist backed by automated checks.

## What is delivered

The deliverable is a final stream, GDSII or OASIS, with a single top cell and all layers mapped by the layer map agreed with the foundry, since the stream identifies layers only by numbers. The die includes a seal ring, a continuous wall of metal and vias at the edge that stops cracks and moisture from the saw lane, and often alignment and identification marks. Supporting data includes the waivers and the signoff reports. Orphan top cells and layer-map mismatches are classic intake failures.

## The signoff checks

Physical signoff requires DRC with the full deck, LVS, antenna, density and ERC, all clean or formally waived. A waiver names the rule and the location it excuses and is agreed with the foundry; it never disables a rule globally. A final XOR between the delivered stream and the signed-off database proves that merging, renaming and conversion did not change geometry. The foundry later derives mask layers from the drawn layers by Booleans and sizing, then applies OPC and fracturing, so drawn-layer correctness is what the designer can guarantee.

## After the handoff

The foundry runs intake checks and its own DRC before committing resources and can return the design. Masks are among the most expensive items in a project, so a respin is costly. Metal-only ECOs exploit spare cells to fix bugs by changing only upper metal masks while reusing the front-end masks. Multi-project wafer shuttles share one mask set among many designs, which is how prototypes and open-source chips reach silicon. Each of these depends on verification being complete and reproducible at handoff.

label: Mask data preparation and fracturing
lesson:
# Mask data preparation and fracturing

Between tape-out and the mask writer lies mask data preparation: deriving mask layers, applying OPC, and fracturing polygons into the simple figures a writer exposes. Data volume and write time grow with the number of figures, not with area. Post-OPC data is far larger than the drawn layout, which is why OASIS and efficient fracturing matter.

## Shot count of a rectangle

A variable-shaped-beam writer exposes one rectangle (or trapezoid) per shot, up to a maximum size $m$. A rectangle $W \times H$ split on a regular grid of maximal shots needs $\lceil W / m \rceil \cdot \lceil H / m \rceil$ shots. A 3200 by 1800 nm rectangle with $m = 1000$ nm needs $4 \cdot 2 = 8$ shots. Writing time is roughly the number of shots times the time per shot, plus settling, so fracturing tries to minimize the count and avoid slivers, very thin shots that print poorly.

## Choosing a fracture

A polygon can be cut into rectangles in different ways, and the shot counts differ. An L-shape, the union of $[0, X] \times [0, Y_1]$ and $[0, X_1] \times [Y_1, Y]$, can be cut horizontally at $y = Y_1$ or vertically at $x = X_1$. Each cut gives two rectangles, each split into shots, and the better cut is the one with fewer shots. The general problem of covering a rectilinear polygon with the fewest rectangles is solved by maximum matching on chords for partitions; with shot-size limits and sliver avoidance, fracturing tools use heuristics.

## Vertex growth after OPC

OPC splits each edge into fragments and moves each fragment independently to pre-compensate printing distortions. A rectangle whose sides of $W$ and $H$ are cut into $m_W = \lceil W/f \rceil$ and $m_H = \lceil H/f \rceil$ fragments of at most $f$ gains a jog of two vertices at every internal break when neighbouring offsets differ: $4 + 2(2(m_W - 1) + 2(m_H - 1))$ vertices. A 400 by 200 nm rectangle with $f = 50$ goes from 4 to $4 + 2(14 + 6) = 44$ vertices. This growth, repeated over billions of shapes, is why mask data sets reach terabytes.

label: Layout XOR between versions
lesson:
# Layout XOR between versions

An XOR compares two versions of a layout: it reports the area covered by exactly one of them. An empty XOR proves two layouts are geometrically identical; a nonzero XOR shows exactly what changed. Tape-out flows XOR the final stream against the signed-off database, and engine developers XOR old and new outputs as a differential test.

## XOR of two shapes

For shapes $A$ and $B$, the XOR area is $|A| + |B| - 2|A \cap B|$. Two rectangles of 120 and 90 square um overlapping in 60 square um give $120 + 90 - 120 = 90$ square um. XOR is a Boolean operation, computed by the same sweep that computes AND and OR. On a layer that should be unchanged, any nonzero XOR stops the flow until someone explains it; on a layer that was edited, the XOR should match the intended edit.

## XOR of two versions of a layer

Real comparisons involve many shapes per version, possibly overlapping within a version. Each version is first merged into its union; the XOR is the area covered by exactly one union. A shape moved by a few units shows up as two thin slivers, not as a whole shape, and a shape added in one version appears in full. XOR engines tile large layouts and run in parallel, and hierarchical XOR compares cells once when both versions share them.

## The signature of a shift

When a $w \times h$ rectangle shifts by $(d_x, d_y)$ with $|d_x| < w$ and $|d_y| < h$, the two copies overlap in a $(w - |d_x|) \times (h - |d_y|)$ box, so the XOR is $2(wh - (w - |d_x|)(h - |d_y|))$. A 100 by 50 rectangle shifted by (3, 0) gives $2(5000 - 4850) = 300$. A whole cell shifted by the same vector produces this signature on every shape, which a reviewer recognizes as a placement change rather than an edit. Tolerances can suppress differences thinner than a threshold, at the risk of hiding real changes.

problems.q: A tape-out XOR compares a shape in the signed-off layout, $[16, 27] \times [16, 30]$, with the same shape in the final stream, $[9, 19] \times [2, 21]$ (um). What area, in square um, does the XOR report?
problems.e: XOR = A + B - 2 (A AND B) = 154 + 190 - 2 x 15 = 314 square um. Any nonzero XOR on a layer that should be unchanged stops the tape-out until it is explained.

problems.q: A tape-out XOR compares a shape in the signed-off layout, $[13, 25] \times [2, 16]$, with the same shape in the final stream, $[11, 29] \times [12, 19]$ (um). What area, in square um, does the XOR report?
problems.e: XOR = A + B - 2 (A AND B) = 168 + 126 - 2 x 48 = 198 square um. Any nonzero XOR on a layer that should be unchanged stops the tape-out until it is explained.

problems.q: A tape-out XOR compares a shape in the signed-off layout, $[9, 25] \times [5, 21]$, with the same shape in the final stream, $[3, 10] \times [1, 6]$ (um). What area, in square um, does the XOR report?
problems.e: XOR = A + B - 2 (A AND B) = 256 + 35 - 2 x 1 = 289 square um. Any nonzero XOR on a layer that should be unchanged stops the tape-out until it is explained.

problems.q: Version 1 of a layer is A1 = $[18, 30] \times [8, 21]$, A2 = $[1, 14] \times [9, 21]$ and version 2 is B1 = $[20, 32] \times [11, 24]$, B2 = $[4, 17] \times [9, 21]$ (um). Shapes within a version may overlap and are merged first. What is the XOR area between the two versions, in square um?
problems.e: Merge each version, then sum the area covered by exactly one of the two unions: 184 square um. A shape moved by a few units shows up as two thin slivers, not as a whole shape.

problems.q: Version 1 of a layer is A1 = $[6, 11] \times [6, 10]$, A2 = $[23, 30] \times [6, 18]$ and version 2 is B1 = $[9, 14] \times [3, 7]$, B2 = $[23, 30] \times [9, 21]$ (um). Shapes within a version may overlap and are merged first. What is the XOR area between the two versions, in square um?
problems.e: Merge each version, then sum the area covered by exactly one of the two unions: 78 square um. A shape moved by a few units shows up as two thin slivers, not as a whole shape.

problems.q: Version 1 of a layer is A1 = $[21, 30] \times [6, 12]$, A2 = $[14, 25] \times [21, 30]$, A3 = $[19, 23] \times [17, 23]$ and version 2 is B1 = $[23, 32] \times [3, 9]$, B2 = $[14, 25] \times [22, 31]$, B3 = $[19, 23] \times [15, 21]$ (um). Shapes within a version may overlap and are merged first. What is the XOR area between the two versions, in square um?
problems.e: Merge each version, then sum the area covered by exactly one of the two unions: 96 square um. A shape moved by a few units shows up as two thin slivers, not as a whole shape.

problems.q: An ECO accidentally shifts a 153 by 84 nm rectangle by (-3, 0) nm. What XOR area, in square nm, does the comparison against the previous version report for that shape?
problems.e: The two copies overlap in a (153 - 3) by (84 - 0) box, so XOR = 2 x (12852 - 12600) = 504. A uniform shift of a whole cell gives the same signature on every shape, which helps a reviewer recognize it.

problems.q: An ECO accidentally shifts a 142 by 157 nm rectangle by (-3, 6) nm. What XOR area, in square nm, does the comparison against the previous version report for that shape?
problems.e: The two copies overlap in a (142 - 3) by (157 - 6) box, so XOR = 2 x (22294 - 20989) = 2610. A uniform shift of a whole cell gives the same signature on every shape, which helps a reviewer recognize it.

problems.q: An ECO accidentally shifts a 73 by 107 nm rectangle by (9, -8) nm. What XOR area, in square nm, does the comparison against the previous version report for that shape?
problems.e: The two copies overlap in a (73 - 9) by (107 - 8) box, so XOR = 2 x (7811 - 6336) = 2950. A uniform shift of a whole cell gives the same signature on every shape, which helps a reviewer recognize it.

label: KLayout, Magic and Netgen in practice
lesson:
# KLayout, Magic and Netgen in practice

Open-source physical verification rests on three tools. KLayout is a layout viewer and editor with DRC and LVS engines scripted in a Ruby-based language. Magic is an interactive layout editor built on corner stitching with continuous DRC and extraction. Netgen compares netlists for LVS. Together with open PDKs such as SKY130 and GF180MCU, they form the signoff layer of flows like OpenLane.

## KLayout

KLayout reads and writes GDSII and OASIS and serves as the common viewer for both. Its DRC and LVS engines are driven by scripts in a Ruby-based domain-specific language: input layers, derived layers by Booleans and sizing, checks such as width and space with a choice of metric, and output markers in a results database. Deep mode processes the layout hierarchically; tiled mode splits flat work into tiles for parallelism. Its LVS extracts devices and connectivity from layer rules and compares the result with a SPICE netlist.

## Magic

Magic stores each layer plane as corner-stitched tiles, which cover empty space as well as material and are linked at their corners, so local queries and edits are fast. Its design rules live in the technology file as edge-based rules, and it rechecks the edited region continuously, showing errors while the user draws. Magic also extracts layouts into its own extraction format, converted to SPICE for LVS and simulation. In open flows Magic often serves as a second, independent DRC and as the extractor feeding Netgen.

## Netgen and the open flow

Netgen compares two netlists, typically the extracted layout and the schematic, by iterative partition refinement with tie-breaking for symmetric classes. Its setup file sets comparison policy: property tolerances, permutable pins, and parallel or series merging. OpenLane uses Magic for DRC and extraction, Netgen for LVS, and KLayout for checks such as an XOR between streams written by different tools. Open PDKs ship decks for these tools, which makes the whole signoff flow inspectable, and a usable base for agent benchmarks that cannot use confidential decks.

## Going deeper

The KLayout documentation for DRC and LVS; the Magic and Netgen documentation; the OpenLane documentation.

label: Agentic DRC fix loops
lesson:
# Agentic DRC fix loops

Signoff DRC on a large block can report thousands of violations after routing. An agentic fix loop reads the report, classifies each violation, routes it to the engine that owns the geometry, reruns the checks and iterates, with a human approving the final ECO. The engineering lies in classification and routing: most violations should go back to an engine as a small, safe change, not be patched by hand.

## Routing violations to the right fixer

Each violation has an owner. Spacing, shorts, minimum area and via enclosure on routed metal belong to the detailed router, which can rerun the affected region with the marker as a blockage or penalty: a Tier 1 action. Antenna violations go to the antenna-repair step, density windows to the fill step, and anything inside a standard-cell or macro layout is escalated, because the router treats those layouts as fixed. A report with 35 spacing (none inside cells), 10 short, 22 minimum-area and 4 enclosure violations sends 71 to the router. The policy is a table, so the agent's routing step is cheap and auditable.

## Classifying violations

Good classification looks for patterns before fixing instances. The same minimum-area violation on hundreds of nets after a router update points to a missing or wrong rule in the router's configuration: one Tier 1 config fix, not hundreds of patches. Markers for a rule the foundry removed point to a stale deck version. A violation inside vendor IP is outside the change surface. Rule names, layers, cell context and repetition across nets are the features a classifier reads, and all of them come from the results database, not from the deck's protected text.

## Closing the loop safely

An agent's change is accepted only when full signoff DRC and LVS pass and a differential run shows no new markers: DRC-clean and LVS-clean are the golden tests. Fixes go through the engines that own the data, never through direct polygon edits to the stream, which would make the design database, extraction and timing disagree with the layout. Reroutes change parasitics, so extraction and timing rerun before signoff. The loop is bounded: if the violation count stops falling (120, 40, 38, 41, 39), the agent stops and escalates the rest.

problems.q:
A signoff DRC report lists 16 metal spacing, 3 short, 11 minimum-area and 8 via-enclosure violations on routed metal, 9 antenna violations and 1 density-window violations. Of the spacing violations, 4 lie entirely inside standard-cell layouts. The agent's policy: violations on routed metal go back to the detailed router as a Tier 1 rerun of the affected region; antenna violations go to the antenna-repair step; density goes to the fill step; anything inside a cell layout is escalated to a human. How many violations does the agent send to the router?

A) 38

B) 34

C) 43

D) 48
problems.e: Routed-metal violations: (16 - 4) + 3 + 11 + 8 = 34. The 4 in-cell spacing violations are not the router's to fix: the router treats cell layouts as fixed, so changing them is a core library change.

problems.q:
A signoff DRC report lists 45 metal spacing, 8 short, 21 minimum-area and 2 via-enclosure violations on routed metal, 4 antenna violations and 1 density-window violations. Of the spacing violations, 2 lie entirely inside standard-cell layouts. The agent's policy: violations on routed metal go back to the detailed router as a Tier 1 rerun of the affected region; antenna violations go to the antenna-repair step; density goes to the fill step; anything inside a cell layout is escalated to a human. How many violations does the agent send to the router?

A) 81

B) 74

C) 78

D) 76
problems.e: Routed-metal violations: (45 - 2) + 8 + 21 + 2 = 74. The 2 in-cell spacing violations are not the router's to fix: the router treats cell layouts as fixed, so changing them is a core library change.

problems.q:
A signoff DRC report lists 32 metal spacing, 3 short, 15 minimum-area and 14 via-enclosure violations on routed metal, 5 antenna violations and 3 density-window violations. Of the spacing violations, 7 lie entirely inside standard-cell layouts. The agent's policy: violations on routed metal go back to the detailed router as a Tier 1 rerun of the affected region; antenna violations go to the antenna-repair step; density goes to the fill step; anything inside a cell layout is escalated to a human. How many violations does the agent send to the router?

A) 64

B) 72

C) 62

D) 57
problems.e: Routed-metal violations: (32 - 7) + 3 + 15 + 14 = 57. The 7 in-cell spacing violations are not the router's to fix: the router treats cell layouts as fixed, so changing them is a core library change.

problems.q:
Markers appear for a rule that the foundry removed in the latest deck. What should the agent check first?

A) The router's cost function

B) The netlist

C) Which deck version the run used

D) The fill density
problems.a: Which deck version the run used
problems.e: A stale deck produces false violations. Fixing layout for a rule that no longer exists wastes work and can harm yield.

problems.q:
After a router update, the same minimum-area violation appears on hundreds of nets. What is the best classification?

A) A systematic router configuration issue, fixed once in the router's rule settings rather than net by net

B) Hundreds of independent random errors

C) An LVS short

D) A density problem
problems.a: A systematic router configuration issue, fixed once in the router's rule settings rather than net by net
problems.e: A pattern across many markers points to a cause upstream. One Tier 1 config fix beats hundreds of patches.

problems.q:
A violation lies inside a hard macro supplied by an IP vendor. What should the agent do?

A) Reroute the macro's internal wires

B) Add fill on top of it

C) Delete the macro shapes near the marker

D) Escalate it: the macro's layout is not the router's to change
problems.a: Escalate it: the macro's layout is not the router's to change
problems.e: Fixed IP is outside the agent's change surface; only the owner can change it or obtain a waiver.

problems.q:
When should an agent's DRC fix be accepted?

A) When the router finishes without error

B) When the fast predictor reports zero hotspots

C) When the marker it targeted disappears

D) When the full signoff DRC and LVS pass and the differential run shows no new markers
problems.a: When the full signoff DRC and LVS pass and the differential run shows no new markers
problems.e: DRC-clean and LVS-clean are the golden tests. A local fix that adds markers elsewhere or breaks connectivity is not a fix.

problems.q:
After the agent reroutes 200 nets to fix spacing, what else must be rerun before signoff?

A) Extraction and timing, because the reroutes changed parasitics

B) Nothing else

C) Floorplanning

D) Synthesis
problems.a: Extraction and timing, because the reroutes changed parasitics
problems.e: DRC fixes change wires, which changes RC. The ECO loop closes only when timing is clean too, with a human approving the final ECO.

problems.q:
The violation count goes 120, 40, 38, 41, 39 over five agent iterations. What should the loop do?

A) Keep iterating indefinitely

B) Revert to the first iteration

C) Waive all remaining violations

D) Stop and escalate the remaining violations, since the loop has stopped converging
problems.a: Stop and escalate the remaining violations, since the loop has stopped converging
problems.e: A bounded loop with a progress test avoids oscillation; the remaining hard cases go to a human.

label: Change tiers for verification engines
lesson:
# Change tiers for verification engines

Verification engines follow the same four-layer model as implementation engines: an immutable geometry and matching core, policies such as check plug-ins and device extractors, parameters such as rule values and switches, and observation hooks over results. Requests arrive constantly from foundries, customers and agents. Landing each at the smallest safe tier keeps the core stable and the engine trustworthy.

## Tier 1 changes in verification

Most verification changes are data. A new deck version raising metal 2 spacing from 40 to 42 nm changes a rule value. A waiver for a known-good IP violation is an entry in a waiver file. Running only antenna checks is a rule selection, and a new density window size and step are check parameters. None of these touch engine code, and none need a rebuild. In a well-designed verification engine the deck is the configuration layer, so a foundry update should be Tier 1 by construction.

## Tier 2 plug-ins

Some requests need new logic but not new core. A via spacing rule that depends on how many neighbouring vias lie within 100 nm, which the deck language cannot express, can be a custom check written against the engine's spatial query API. A custom capacitor needs a device-extractor plug-in that names its recognition layers and terminals. A team-specific property comparison is a hook in LVS. Exporting results as typed records for an agent is an observation hook. Each plug-in sees plain data, runs in a sandbox, and must pass golden tests on reference layouts.

## Tier 3 core edits

Core edits change what every check relies on: the Boolean and sizing kernel, exact predicates, hierarchy and context handling, the coordinate width, the matching algorithm. A wrong result on 45-degree edges is a core bug, fixed with a human-approved diff and full regression, never patched by a plug-in that post-processes outputs. A seam is in the right place when Tier 3 edits essentially never happen for a class of request. If customers keep needing core edits for variants of end-of-line rules, the engine is missing a parameterized rule family or a check extension point.

problems.q:
A team wants to waive one known-good violation inside a qualified IP block. Which tier?

A) Tier 1: an entry in the waiver configuration

B) Edit the IP layout

C) Tier 2: a new check

D) Tier 3: a core change to result handling
problems.a: Tier 1: an entry in the waiver configuration
problems.e: Waivers are data that the engine already understands.

problems.q:

A) Tier 2: write a new antenna engine

B) Tier 1: select rules through deck switches or a rule selection

C) Tier 3: modify the hierarchy handler

D) It is impossible
problems.a: Tier 1: select rules through deck switches or a rule selection
problems.e: Selecting checks is a run option. No new code is involved.

A) Tier 3: a change to the Boolean core

B) Tier 2: a new density algorithm

C) A layout change

D) Tier 1: window size and step are parameters of the density check
problems.a: Tier 1: window size and step are parameters of the density check
problems.e: Density engines take window and step as parameters.

A) A layout edit

B) A new rule in the deck

C) A core change to the checker

D) An observation hook or output plug-in over the results database
problems.a: An observation hook or output plug-in over the results database
problems.e: Exposing results to an agent is reading state, which is what observation hooks are for.

problems.q:

B) An observation hook or output plug-in over the results database

C) A layout edit

D) A new rule in the deck
problems.a: An observation hook or output plug-in over the results database
problems.e: Exposing results to an agent is reading state, which is what observation hooks are for.

problems.q:

A) Tier 2: a device-extractor plug-in that defines its recognition layers and terminals

B) Tier 3: change the netlist comparison core

C) Tier 1: rename a layer

D) Waive the device
problems.a: Tier 2: a device-extractor plug-in that defines its recognition layers and terminals
problems.e: Device extractors are a natural extension point: recognition and property measurement vary, comparison does not.

problems.q:
The Boolean engine produces wrong output on some 45-degree edges. Which tier is the fix, and what does it require?

A) Tier 1: a deck option

B) Tier 2: a plug-in that post-processes results

C) Tier 3: a core edit, with a human-approved diff and full regression

D) No fix; waive the markers
problems.a: Tier 3: a core edit, with a human-approved diff and full regression
problems.e: Correctness of the geometry kernel is core. A plug-in that patches outputs would hide the bug.

label: Clean results as golden and differential tests
lesson:
# Clean results as golden and differential tests

For physical verification, the golden test is simple to state: the reference designs must stay DRC-clean and LVS-clean, and the regression designs must produce exactly the expected markers. Differential runs compare marker sets before and after a change. Counting what was introduced, what was fixed and what merely moved is the core of judging an agent's fix or an engine change.

## Introduced markers

A marker is a rule name plus a location. With exact matching, a new-run marker is introduced if no baseline marker has the same rule and position. If the baseline has five markers and the new run has six, of which three match baseline markers exactly, then three were introduced. An accepted fix must introduce none, whatever it did to the old ones: a fix that clears its target marker but adds one elsewhere is a regression. Engines key markers by rule and cell coordinates so that hierarchical results compare across runs.

## Fixed markers

A baseline marker is fixed if it no longer appears in the new run. A marker of the same rule at a different location is a new violation, not the old one moved, so it counts on both sides: one fixed, one introduced. The pair (fixed, introduced) summarizes a change better than the total count, which can stay flat while the layout gets worse. For engine changes rather than layout changes, the expected answer on a regression suite is zero fixed and zero introduced, unless the change was meant to alter results.

## Matching with tolerance

Reruns can shift a marker slightly, through different tiling or sliver handling, without any real change. Differential tools therefore match markers of the same rule within a tolerance, for example a Manhattan distance of at most 3 nm. A marker moved by 2 nm still matches; one moved by 5 nm is unmatched and counts as introduced. Too small a tolerance turns jitter into false regressions, too large one hides real moves. The tolerance is a Tier 1 parameter of the differential check, chosen from the engine's known numerical behaviour.

label: Fast hotspot prediction versus signoff
prereqs: Fast and accurate engines in a modeling loop
lesson:
# Fast hotspot prediction versus signoff

Learned hotspot predictors are the fast engine of lithography verification: milliseconds per clip against seconds for simulation. An agent can use them inside a modeling loop, but signoff still belongs to the accurate engine. The questions are how much the fast path saves, what it misses, and how a reward built on it can be gamed.

## Screen then verify

Run the predictor on all $N$ clips at $t_m$ each and simulate only the $k$ flagged ones at $t_s$ each. The speedup over simulating everything is $N t_s / (N t_m + k t_s)$. With $N = 10000$, $t_m = 2$ ms, $t_s = 2400$ ms and $k = 1200$, the speedup is $24000000 / 2900000 = 8.3$. The flag rate bounds the gain: as $k / N$ grows, simulation dominates again. A predictor tuned for very high recall flags more clips, so recall and speedup trade against each other.

## Escapes at a threshold

A predictor outputs a score, and the agent sends clips scoring at least a threshold to simulation. A true hotspot scoring below the threshold escapes if nothing else checks it. With scores and labels from a later full run, count the hotspots below the threshold: those are the false negatives. Lowering the threshold catches more but sends more clips to simulation. Because escapes become yield loss, the fast screen can steer an agent's choices during the loop, but the final signoff must run the accurate engine on the whole layout.

## Gaming the proxy

If an agent is rewarded for lowering the predicted hotspot count, it can learn edits that move layouts into the predictor's blind spots. Precision and recall translate a predicted count into an expected real count: with $P$ predictions, true positives are $P \cdot \text{precision}$, and those are a fraction recall of the real hotspots, so the real count is about $P \cdot \text{precision} / \text{recall}$. With 159 predictions, precision 0.52 and recall 0.8, expect about 103 real hotspots. A tool-grounded reward must therefore be checked periodically against simulation, and the predictor's recall on the agent's own outputs re-measured.

label: Rule decks and the IP boundary
lesson:
# Rule decks and the IP boundary

Physical verification touches the most sensitive data in the chain: the foundry's rule decks, device recognition and hotspot libraries, and the customer's complete layout. An agent working on DRC or LVS must operate inside a boundary that keeps all of it on site. The boundary is part of the architecture: what the agent may read, where it runs, what it may log, and what can flow back as shared know-how.

## Whose IP is whose

Rule decks, device models and pattern libraries are foundry IP, licensed under NDA to customers and tool vendors; they encode process capability. Some decks are delivered encrypted so that only the checking tool can read them. The layout and netlists are the customer's IP. An agent can work from rule names, marker locations and measured values in the results, plus the design-rule documentation available under the same agreement. Reading protected deck text by other means would breach the license.

## Architecture of the boundary

The agent drives the engines through typed tool interfaces running in a sandbox with no network access, on site. Logs sent anywhere are redacted of coordinates, cell and net names and geometry. Models fine-tuned on one customer's layouts may memorize them, so they must not serve another customer. Foundry pattern libraries cannot be bundled into skills shared across customers. These rules are enforced by the harness, not left to the model's discretion.

## Boundary decisions in practice

Concrete requests test the boundary. Sending failing clips to a cloud hotspot service is a transfer of design data, so the agent uses the on-site predictor or simulation instead. A fix strategy learned at one customer can be promoted to the shared library only as generic logic that passes golden and differential tests on reference designs, without that customer's data. Public benchmarks for agentic DRC use open PDKs such as SKY130 and GF180MCU or synthetic layouts. Quoting a confidential rule to a licensed user inside the deployment is acceptable; letting it reach a shared log or training set is not.
